source_read: PDF, Drug and Alcohol Dependence 72 (2003) 67-74, all 8 pages read (pdftotext -layout). Text pages 67-69 checked on renders at 150 dpi; the rotated Tables 2 (p. 71) and 3 (p. 72) have a scrambled text layer, so they were read only on renders at 200 and 300 dpi, rotated, as were the text columns of pp. 71-72.

claims.overstatement: None. The three figures are correctly labelled 'as cited by Webb et al.' (second-hand: Home Office bulletin, NP-SAD, ONS). They differ in year (2000 against 1999) and definition (coroners' drug-misuse verdicts; deaths reported to a voluntary register; all-intent drug-poisoning underlying cause) and are not linked records, so they illustrate that counts differ, not how far the same deaths overlap; the claim does not say otherwise. 'The same register' holds only if the Liverpool register in the preceding sentence (Beynon et al., 2007) is the NP-SAD; within Webb, the 1,296 is the NP-SAD's count.
claims.note: 605, 1,296 and 2,943 found on p. 67 and confirmed on the rendered page; 605 was up 5% from 573 (605/573 = 1.056).

anchors.locator: 1. Introduction, 2nd paragraph (right column of p. 67, ending at the top of p. 68)
anchors.extracted: As cited: coroners' verdicts of death from drug misuse rose 5% in 2000, from 573 to 605 (Allen, 2001, Home Office bulletin); the NP-SAD recorded 1,296 drug-related deaths in 2000; the ONS reported 2,943 deaths in England and Wales in 1999 with drug poisoning as the underlying cause. The authors put the widely differing figures down to variation in data collection and recording.

anchors.locator: 2. Methods > 2.1 The NP-SAD database; 4. Discussion, 6th (last) paragraph
anchors.extracted: The NP-SAD takes coroners' returns from England and Wales: drug-related deaths in which a psychoactive substance was directly implicated, where the person had a history of dependence or abuse. Coroners supply demographics, prescribed medication, circumstances, substances found after death, the verdict and the certified causes. Reporting to the NP-SAD is voluntary, and there is no standardized system of toxicological testing and reporting at inquest.

claims.overstatement: Slight wording issue: 'the rest sudden events such as breathing in stomach contents (74), drug toxicity on top of a medical condition (112), injuries (31) and infections (18)' puts medical conditions and infections under 'sudden events'. Only the 'acute physical event' category (74) is a sudden event in the paper's terms. 'The rest other mechanisms: ...' would fit. Also, 'direct overdose' was the default category when nothing suggested otherwise, so 77% is the most and 23% the least that the coroners' returns allowed for each.
claims.note: 1,037 = 802 + 31 + 40 + 72 + 18 + 74; 802/1,037 = 77.3%; 40 + 72 = 112. The comparison with official statistics is indeed absent: the paper compares no record with ONS data.

anchors.extracted: 1,037 accidental drug-related deaths reported in 2000; 802 (77%) classed as direct acute overdose; the other 23%: traumatic accident 31 (3%), toxicity on a non-drug-related medical condition 40 (4%), toxicity on a drug-related medical condition 72 (7%), acute infection 18 (2%), acute non-traumatic physical event 74 (7%).

anchors.locator: 2. Methods > 2.2 Case identification; 2.3 Case categorisation, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Deaths were classed as accidental and as direct overdose when no evidence suggested otherwise. Suicide verdicts, open verdicts with clear suicidal or homicidal intent, no verdict, and cases with too little information for a causal judgement were excluded. Categories followed a hierarchy of evidence: certified cause, coroner's verdict, drugs implicated, drugs found after death, then the coroner's description.

anchors.locator: 2. Methods > 2.3 Case categorisation, last paragraph; 3. Results > 3.1 Concordance ratings
anchors.extracted: Two researchers classified cases independently and an addiction consultant confirmed the categories. Agreement (phi) was 0.77 overall: 0.85 direct overdose, 0.92 traumatic accident, 0.88 acute event, 0.72 medical conditions and 0.64 acute infection (11 of 18 agreed).

claims.overstatement: None for the Webb part; it is scoped to accidental register deaths, calls the categories the researchers' reading, and notes that no official statistics were compared. Omissions: (1) 'direct overdose' was the default when nothing suggested otherwise (p. 68), so the 23% other mechanisms is a floor, given what coroners returned; (2) the Discussion states that a third of direct overdose cases had heroin/morphine as the only drug implicated (p. 72), a figure on 'heroin alone' that the claim does not use. Its referent is ambiguous (a third of all direct overdoses, or of those with heroin/morphine) and the tables give no sole-drug column; (3) alcohol is recorded only when found with other drugs, so 316 (39.4%) means alcohol with other substances.
claims.note: All numbers recomputed: 235 = 74 + 112 + 31 + 18; 424/802 = 52.9%; 488/802 = 60.8%; 42/74 = 56.8%; 33/72 = 45.8%; 11/18 = 61.1%; 316/802 = 39.4%; methadone 101/802 = 12.6% (13%). The 4% sole-drug methadone figure appears only in the text (pp. 71, 72). Heroin/morphine was found after death but not implicated in 64 direct overdoses (488 - 424; editors' calculation). Table 2 has internal errors that do not touch the claim's figures (see the card check).

anchors.locator: 3. Results > 3.2 Causes of death, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Of 1,037 accidental deaths, 802 (77%) were direct overdoses and 235 other mechanisms: acute non-traumatic physical event 74, drug-related medical condition 72, non-drug-related medical condition 40, traumatic accident 31, acute infection 18. Within acute events, aspiration of gastric contents was mentioned in 42 direct aspiration asphyxias and 22 aspiration pneumonias, with 6 postural asphyxias and 1 hypothermia; 11 road traffic accidents.

anchors.locator: Table 2 (implicated substance by manner of death), heroin/morphine, methadone and alcohol rows
anchors.extracted: Heroin/morphine implicated, alone or with other drugs: direct overdose 424 of 802 (53%), acute physical event 42 of 74 (57%), drug-related medical condition 33 of 72 (46%), acute infection 11 of 18 (61%), non-drug-related medical condition 9 of 40, traumatic accident 9 of 31. Methadone implicated in 101 (13%) of direct overdoses. Alcohol, recorded only with other substances, was implicated in 232 (29%).

anchors.locator: Table 3 (drug found post mortem by manner of death), direct overdose column
anchors.extracted: Found after death in direct overdoses (n = 802): heroin/morphine 488 (60.8%); alcohol, with other substances, 316 (39.4%); hypnotic/sedative 220 (27.4%); other opiates 168 (20.9%); methadone 112 (14.0%); cocaine 74 (9.2%).

anchors.locator: 3.4 Substances implicated in death and cause of death, 2nd paragraph; 4. Discussion, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Methadone was implicated in 13% of direct overdoses but was the sole drug implicated in 4%, and 14% of direct overdoses were positive for it. Heroin/morphine was implicated in over half of all accidental deaths and of direct overdoses; the Discussion adds that a third of direct overdose cases had taken only heroin/morphine. Sole-drug figures appear only in the text.

anchors.locator: 2. Methods > 2.2 Case identification; 2.3 Case categorisation, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Direct overdose was the default category for accidental deaths with recent drug use when nothing suggested another cause. Classification used, in order, the certified cause, the verdict, drugs implicated, drugs found after death and the coroner's description; suicides, open verdicts with clear intent, no verdict and cases with insufficient information were excluded.

The NP-SAD records alcohol only when present or implicated with other drugs. Coroners report voluntarily, there is no standardized toxicological testing or reporting at inquest, and returns list substances found, so it is unclear whether a substance not reported was absent or not tested for.

reporting_issues.note: Checked on the rendered Table 1 (p. 70): female direct overdose 0.3 carries footnote a (CI above 1.0); no-fixed-abode 0.8, 0.6, 0.6, 0.4; history of misuse 0.9 for drug-related medical condition; employed 1.1 for traumatic accident.
Found independently on the 300 dpi render of Table 2: other opiates 7 (5), methadone 20 (19), anti-psychotic 4 (4), alcohol 21 (27); cocaine in acute infection 2 (1).

risk_of_bias.note: High is defensible. For the category counts that the claims use, the concern is mainly unknown coverage and the researchers' unvalidated, default-driven classification, not the prevalence-ratio statistics behind domain 8.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's 'masked' manner of death rests on no comparison with how the deaths were certified or coded, and the risk language rests on within-category percentages.

missed: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 72): a third of direct overdose cases had taken only heroin/morphine. This sole-drug figure bears on claims about heroin alone; its referent is ambiguous (a third of all direct overdoses, or of those with heroin/morphine) and no table gives sole-drug counts.

Because direct overdose was the default category when nothing suggested otherwise (p. 68, 2.2), the 77% direct-overdose share is an upper bound and the 23% other mechanisms a lower bound, given the detail in coroners' returns. This complements reporting issue 0, which reads the same rule as a conflict of definitions.
